metadata.title: 2007 Case 16
metadata.original_presentation: A 61-year-old man was referred to the thoracic oncology service of this hospital for management of a thymoma.

required.content: What was the initial symptom that led to the patient's hospital visit?
required.response: The patient experienced the sudden onset of sharp left anterior chest pain, which was worse adjacent to the sternum and when he took a deep breath.

teaching_points.content: Chest pain can be a symptom of various conditions, including cardiac, pulmonary, and mediastinal pathologies.

required.content: What is the patient's past medical history?
required.response: The patient was obese, had hypertension and hypercholesterolemia, had undergone parathyroidectomy for hyperparathyroidism, had been treated for Lyme disease, developed Guillain–Barré syndrome after a tetanus toxoid injection, and had undergone neck irradiation for pertussis in childhood.

teaching_points.content: A comprehensive medical history can provide insights into potential risk factors and comorbidities that may affect diagnosis and treatment.

required.content: What is the patient's smoking history?
required.response: The patient had smoked cigarettes for 25 years and had quit smoking 20 years earlier.

teaching_points.content: Smoking history is important in assessing risk for various cancers and respiratory conditions.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Thymoma
supporting_evidence: referred to thoracic oncology for management of a thymoma
additional_information_needed: imaging studies to confirm size and extent

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Pulmonary Embolism
supporting_evidence: sudden onset of sharp left anterior chest pain, worse with deep breath
refuting_evidence: no mention of risk factors like recent surgery or immobilization

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Acute Coronary Syndrome
key_features: risk factors include hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, smoking history
supporting_evidence: sharp chest pain
history of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia
refuting_evidence: pain is pleuritic and not typical for ACS

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Costochondritis
supporting_evidence: sharp left anterior chest pain, worse adjacent to the sternum
refuting_evidence: no mention of tenderness on palpation
additional_information_needed: physical examination focusing on chest wall tenderness

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Pleuritis
supporting_evidence: chest pain worse with deep breath
refuting_evidence: no mention of recent respiratory infection or fever

required.content: What were the findings on physical examination?
required.response: The patient's vital signs were normal. He had a body-mass index of 37. There was no jugular venous distention, cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. The chest was clear on auscultation, and there was no tenderness on palpation of the ribs or sternum. The remainder of the examination was normal.

teaching_points.content: A thorough physical examination can help rule out other potential causes of symptoms and assess the patient's overall health status.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Thymoma
supporting_evidence: referred to thoracic oncology for management of a thymoma
sudden onset of sharp left anterior chest pain
additional_information_needed: imaging studies such as CT or MRI of the chest

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Pulmonary Embolism
key_features: risk factors such as obesity and smoking history
supporting_evidence: sudden onset of sharp chest pain worse on deep breath

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Acute Coronary Syndrome
key_features: risk factors such as hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and smoking history
supporting_evidence: sudden onset of chest pain
refuting_evidence: no tenderness on palpation of the chest

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Costochondritis
key_features: chest pain localized to the costosternal, costochondral, or costovertebral joints
pain worsens with movement or palpation
supporting_evidence: sharp anterior chest pain
refuting_evidence: no tenderness on palpation of the ribs or sternum

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Pericarditis
supporting_evidence: sharp chest pain
refuting_evidence: no mention of positional changes affecting pain

required.content: What imaging studies were performed and what were the findings?
required.response: CT scanning of the chest revealed a lobulated, soft-tissue mass in the left anterior mediastinum. An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET scan showed intense focal uptake within the mass, suggesting a malignant condition. A whole-body PET scan showed increased uptake of tracer in the area of the lesion, with no other areas of increased uptake. A bone scan was negative.

teaching_points.content: Imaging studies are crucial in identifying and characterizing masses, and PET scans can help assess metabolic activity indicative of malignancy.

required.content: What were the results of pulmonary-function testing?
required.response: The results were consistent with moderate mixed obstructive and restrictive disease, with a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 1.96 (56% of the predicted value) and a forced vital capacity of 3.12 (59% of the predicted value).

teaching_points.content: Pulmonary function tests can help assess the impact of thoracic masses on respiratory function.

required.content: What were the findings from the bronchoscopic examination?
required.response: The bronchoscopic examination showed no endobronchial lesions.

teaching_points.content: Bronchoscopy can be used to visualize the airways and rule out endobronchial involvement in thoracic masses.

required.response: Mediastinoscopy and biopsy of mediastinal lymph nodes revealed no malignant tumor. A left anterior mediastinal exploration with biopsy showed a poorly circumscribed mass invading the pericardium, diagnosed as a predominantly cortical, type B1 thymoma.

teaching_points.content: Biopsy is essential for histological diagnosis and can guide treatment decisions.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Thymoma
supporting_evidence: CT scan showing lobulated mass in left anterior mediastinum
Intense focal uptake on PET scan
Biopsy showing type B1 thymoma

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Lung cancer
supporting_evidence: History of smoking for 25 years
Intense focal uptake on PET scan
refuting_evidence: Biopsy showing thymoma, not lung cancer
additional_information_needed: Further histological examination to rule out lung cancer

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Lymphoma
supporting_evidence: Intense focal uptake on PET scan
additional_information_needed: Further histological examination to rule out lymphoma

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Mediastinal germ cell tumor
supporting_evidence: Anterior mediastinal mass
refuting_evidence: Patient's age is older than typical presentation

required.content: What management decision was made for the patient?
required.response: The patient was referred to the hospital for further treatment of the thymoma.

teaching_points.content: Referral to a specialized center can be important for the management of complex cases such as thymoma.

final_diagnosis.name: Type B1 Thymoma
key_features: Lobulated, soft-tissue mass in the left anterior mediastinum
Intense focal uptake on PET scan
Biopsy confirmed predominantly cortical, type B1 thymoma
supporting_evidence: CT and PET scan findings
Biopsy results
